lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.unitTitle: Complex Solutions, Polynomials, and the Binomial Theorem
lessonRef.focus: extending polynomial identities to the complex numbers
lessonRef.title: Launch and diagnostic: extending polynomial identities to the complex numbers

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Read the example first. You are not expected to know this yet.

items.prompt: Factor x² + 9 over the complex numbers.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Try each one. If you get stuck, write what you do know and move on.

items.prompt: A polynomial with real coefficients has degree 3. How many roots does it have in the complex numbers, counted with multiplicity, and what constrains its non-real roots?
choices: exactly 2, and any non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs
exactly 6, and any non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs
exactly 4, and any non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs
exactly 3, and any non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs

items.prompt: In the expansion of (x + y)^4, find the coefficient of the term x^2·y^2.
Complete the statement: the sum of two rational expressions …
choices: need not be a rational expression, because the denominators may differ
is always a rational expression, because dividing is multiplying by the reciprocal
is always a rational expression, because numerators and denominators multiply directly
is always a rational expression, because a common denominator can always be formed

items.prompt: Factor x² + 36 completely over the complex numbers.
choices: (x + 6i)²

items.prompt: A polynomial with real coefficients has degree 5. How many roots does it have in the complex numbers, counted with multiplicity, and what constrains its non-real roots?
choices: exactly 4, and any non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs
exactly 6, and any non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs
exactly 5, and any non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs
exactly 3, and any non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Show what you can do so far. This sets the starting point, not a grade.

items.prompt: In the expansion of (x + y)^6, find the coefficient of the term x^5·y^1.
Complete the statement: the quotient of two rational expressions, where the divisor is not the zero expression …
choices: is always a rational expression, because a common denominator can always be formed
is always a rational expression, because dividing is multiplying by the reciprocal
is always a rational expression, because numerators and denominators multiply directly
need not be a rational expression, because the denominators may differ
